catalog_quote: 1.1 Intonation. Intonation contours are distinguished by changes among three pitch levels. Near the end of each contour (determined by pause), the pitch may rise to level /3/, stay at level /2/ (starting point), or rise to level /3/ and drop to level /1/. ... (4) /231/ ... This contour marks the end of a sentence that ends with a two-syllable word. The sentence may be a statement, or a question with an interrogative substitute like nasava 'what?'. Its meaning is the same as that of the following. (5) /2311/ 2natua 3wa1i1na 'that year' 2e taa 3p̄a1ru1a 'It's not big.' This contour marks the end of a sentence that ends with a word of three or more syllables. Isolated forms, given as "words," are accompanied by patterns (4) and (5). This accounts for earlier statements of antepenultimate accent or stress.14 ... [p.79] (d) In the treatment of intonation, no work has yet been done with stres…
readall_conflicts: The only listed work (Capell MS) could not be opened, so no conflict can be established from it. Among the secondary sources already held by the project there is a mild disagreement about how to describe Nguna prominence rather than where it falls: Clark 2025 (Te Reo, p. 309) says Schütz 1969b p. 10 'does not discuss stress as such in Nguna, but finds a falling intonation contour at the end of declarative sentences which places prominence on the antepenultimate syllable', and McClintock 1991 pp. 88-89 describes 'a three-mora measure preference' with greater intensity on the first mora, which Clark 'will consider.. as antepenultimate (V3) stress'; Billington et al. 2020 (JASA 147(4), p. 2831) simply report 'antepenultimate stress in Nguna (Schütz, 1969, p. 11)'. Capell (per Billington 2020) speaks of 'strong stress' in the Efate dialects and of final prominence in varieties with many closed final syllables, which would apply to Nafsan/South Efate rather than Nguna.

audit.recode_to: Pending McClintock 1991: likely fixed antepenultimate (quantity-insensitive, mora/V-CV-syllable counting: antepenult in words of 3+ syllables, penult=initial in disyllables), domain word (phonological word incl. proclitic na-/e-), rather than PHRASAL. At minimum add a caution/contra note now citing Clark 2025 pp.309-310 and McClintock 1991.

(2) The deciding source is an 88-pp 1969 grammar sketch whose author explicitly did not study stress; our PHRASAL coding is a faithful reading of it. But it is not the best available evidence: a web search surfaced Clark 2025 (Te Reo, open, downloaded) which cites McClintock 1991, an instrumental study of Nguna prosody in UH Working Papers in Linguistics 23, as finding a three-mora measure with intensity on the first mora, and Clark himself codes Nguna as antepenultimate (V3) word stress with stress-marked forms (náika, émate, támana, duálima) and field impressions from Sasake/Nguna recordings; Billington et al. 2020 likewise read Schütz p.11 as 'antepenultimate stress'. sources.quote: p.309: 'Schütz (1969b, p. 10) does not discuss stress as such in Nguna, but finds a falling intonation contour at the end of declarative sentences which places prominence on the antepenultimate syllable (Table 31). A more recent study interprets this in terms of "a three-mora measure preference": ś s s with a "greater degree of intensity (dB)" on the first mora (McClintock, 1991, pp. 88-89). I will consider this as antepenultimate (V3) stress.' Table 32 gives stress-marked Nguna forms náika 'fish', é-mate 'dead', é-uta 'landward', támana 'father-3s', duálima 'ten'; 'Nguna in many cases places
